anomaly_def.Name: Query Plan Selection Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Query Plan Selection Anomaly: The optimizer chooses a markedly inefficient execution plan even though statistics are adequate.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions request conflicting locks, leading to prolonged blocking or deadlocks.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Sessions compete for hot buffer-cache pages and latches, stalling on low-level synchronization primitives.

When all three conditions co-exist, the database exhibits a compound failure pattern: an ill-chosen execution plan triggers large scans or explosive join fan-outs that touch many more rows and pages than necessary; these bloated data accesses demand numerous locks and repeated buffer pin/latch operations. As a result, lock-wait queues grow, deadlock reports surge, CPU time is consumed by latch spin/sleep cycles, and overall response times and throughput degrade erratically. Performance counters may simultaneously show optimizer plan churn, escalating lock-wait and deadlock statistics, plus spikes in buffer busy or page-latch waits, making single-root-cause isolation difficult.

Causally, the sub-optimal plan is the spark: by scanning or joining far more rows, it expands the lock footprint and lengthens transaction duration, increasing the window for conflicting lock requests. These prolonged holds, in turn, keep buffer pages pinned and their associated latches occupied, propagating latch contention to other sessions that need the same pages. The resulting latch stalls slow query execution even further, extending lock lifetimes and intensifying lock contention—a feedback loop that can culminate in systemic throughput collapse, widespread deadlocks, and severe latency spikes for transactional workloads.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
